column3: QuickBooks is only reconciled through about January–February 2026. The reconciliation workbook (2026_Bank Reconciliation.xlsx, 43 tabs / ~35 bank accounts) shows March 2026 onward entered on the bank side but the QuickBooks column reads 0 — meaning real activity was never posted to the books.
column4: Partners and the bank are reading numbers that are ~4 months stale. Distributions, loan draws, and decisions get made on bad data, and year-end becomes a fire drill.
column5: We pull bank activity automatically and post a structured monthly catch-up
column6: then keep it current going forward.
column7: Always-current financials you can trust for decisions and lender requests; no year-end scramble; lower CPA bill at tax time.

column3: Specific accounts are flagged "NO QB FILE IMPORT" and are keyed by hand — the STVE and STDG accounts at MACU (Mountain America) and Granite Credit Union. There is no automated bank feed for these.
column4: Hours of manual typing each month and a high chance of transcription errors that later have to be hunted down. STDG-Granite alone is sitting ~$730K unreconciled.
column5: We set up an automated bank-to-QuickBooks data bridge (QODBC / QB Web Connector) so transactions flow in.
column6: Saves bookkeeping hours every month and removes a whole category of typing errors.

column4: Expenses and profit per project are understated by the amounts above; the books don't match the bank.

column3: A $317,137.06 entry sits in "Ask My Accountant" on the HLN Arixa construction loan (Journal Entry #71, dated 10/18/2024) with no explanation. It is the leftover after the loan's $16.1M face is reduced by the $1.45M interest reserve, $13.9M principal, and $432,862.94 of itemized closing costs — i.e. a plug, not a real expense.
column4: The HLN loan balance is misstated by a six-figure amount and a large number is parked in a "we'll figure it out later" account — an audit and lender red flag that erodes trust in the books.
column5: We traced the exact math and proved it's a balancing figure; once the Arixa 10/18/2024 settlement statement is in hand, it gets reclassified to the loan (contra-liability) or capitalized — never expensed, never left in "Ask My Accountant."
column6: Clean and defensible loan balances and an audit trail; removes a major credibility risk with lenders and partners.

column3: A SECOND $800 check to Ricks & Co. CPA on the Rock Creek account cleared 5/05/2026 (bank ID fitid 2daa1928), in addition to the legitimate $800 that cleared 4/08/2026. The second one is not in the workbook and looks like a possible duplicate CPA payment.
column4: The company may have paid the same K-1 filing bill twice — $800 of real cash potentially out the door.
column5: Our process scans the transaction data for duplicates automatically and flags them; this one is flagged ON HOLD pending the check image before anything is booked.
column6: Catches double-payments so we can stop-payment or recover the money — direct cash back to the company. (Action: pull the 5/05 check image to confirm.)

column3: Two different entities share the same last-4 digits: Ventura Landing AND Dominus both end in 17470. (Confirmed which is which: the …17470 with routing [ROUTING-REDACTED] / UCCU and an $86,524.82 ledger tie is Ventura Landing.)
column4: It's easy to post money to the wrong entity on last-4 alone, creating tangled intercompany "Due to/from" balances that take hours to unwind.
column5: We built an entity/account map that flags this collision and forces a full account-number check before posting.
column6: Money lands in the right entity the first time; far fewer intercompany cleanups.

column3: In December 2025 the HLN entity suffered a fraud event. The compromised HLN operating bank account ending …92090 was CLOSED on 12/05/2025 and replaced with a new account ending …48560. The old …92090 account still carries roughly $118,750 that was never cleared off the books — it needs a one-time write-off (loss) or receivable entry to record the fraud loss / expected recovery and zero out the dead account.
column4: A ~$118,750 balance is sitting on a closed, compromised account — assets are overstated, the fraud loss isn't recorded, and any insurance/bank recovery claim isn't being tracked. The new …48560 account also needs to be tied into the books cleanly.
column8: and scoped the correcting journal entry so the loss/receivable is recorded and tracked to recovery.
column10: the closed account is zeroed out
column11: and any recovery from the bank/insurer is actively tracked instead of forgotten.

column3: Key files were scattered loose on a desktop (the bank dataset and the variance booking sheet were sitting unfiled among ~50 unrelated files), and much of how the books work lived only in the outgoing accountant's (Adam's) head.
column4: When Adam leaves, that knowledge walks out the door; time is wasted hunting for files and re-learning the system, and there's no record of why entries were made.
column5: We built one organized project folder plus a written "running memory" that documents the system, every decision, and where each file lives.
column6: Continuity if anyone leaves; no key-person risk; new staff get up to speed fast.

column3: The mid-2025 move from Central Bank to UCCU (Utah Community Credit Union) was never fully carried through in the books, so some accounts have a gap where the old bank stops and the new one hasn't been fully posted.
column4: Reconciliation gaps and missing history make several accounts impossible to tie out cleanly; ~16 accounts still need fresh bank-data pulls (mostly UCCU).
column5: Our catch-up plan pulls the missing UCCU and Central Bank history and closes the gaps in one pass.
column6: Every account ties out cleanly with complete history.

column3: Duplicate and stale report versions are saved throughout the QB-Reports folder (the Arixa journal entry was saved 5 separate times; old "as-of" report copies linger; an empty QB_UPDATING-Reports.xlsx and even a stray Claude Setup.exe were mis-filed in there).
column4: People open the wrong version and make decisions on outdated numbers; clutter hides the current file.
column5: We clean up the clutter and keep one current and clearly-named version of each report.
column6: Everyone works from the one correct number — fewer mistakes.

column3: Weekly partner updates are built by hand in Google Slides for each project — manual, slow, and only as fresh as whoever last updated them.
column4: Hours spent every week rebuilding slides; numbers can be stale or inconsistent between projects, and partners can't dig in on their own.
column5: Recommend a live, auto-updating dashboard (a connected Google Sheet or Looker Studio view per project) that the weekly slides pull from — or that replaces the manual deck entirely.
column6: Partners see real-time, consistent per-project numbers and can self-serve; saves hours of weekly slide-building and removes copy-paste errors. (Keep a simple summary slide for the meeting, but feed it from live data.)
